items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow, code written in advance sets the steps and their order; in an agent, the model decides the next step and when to stop. Model size (a), whether a model is called at all (c), and whether tools are allowed (d) do not separate the two.

Only option c has code fixing the sequence (lookup, one model call, send) the same way for every request. In a, b and d the model chooses the tools, their order or how many calls to make, which is the agent pattern.

Agent: 40 x 5 = 200 calls per day. Workflow: 40 x 2 = 80 calls per day. Difference: 200 - 80 = 120 model calls per day, which is the extra cost of letting the model choose each step when the steps never vary.

When the steps and their order are known in advance and the same every time, a fixed workflow is the better choice: fewer model calls, predictable cost and behaviour, and easy testing. Agents earn their cost when the steps cannot be known ahead. Flexibility is not free (b), an agent does not save calls here (c), and a workflow does not adapt to unplanned requests (d).

In a workflow the order is hard-coded by the team, so check_calendar runs after step 1 whatever the model writes; the model only does the work inside its own steps. Thinking the model chose it (a) mixes up a workflow with an agent, which is the control-flow idea this objective is about.

This is a routing workflow: the model makes one bounded choice among paths the team built, and code runs the fixed steps of each. The model does not choose steps, order or when to stop, so the code still owns the control flow. Using a model (a) or influencing which path runs (b) does not make a system an agent; an agent's model controls the loop itself.
